Chaque jeudi aux alentours de 16 h, dans: Every Thursday around 4 p.m., in the YMCA du Parc gym, the bounce of basketballs from the first players to arrive announces that it's time for the 13-to-16-year-olds' practice.
À 16 h 30 précises, un coup de sifflet m: At 4:30 p.m. sharp, a whistle blast kicks off practice. “Huddle up!” calls Eddy Maurice, the basketball coach, whose graying beard testifies to his 20 years of experience in youth work at various community centres.
Bien qu’il ne se soit joint au YMCA qu’e: Although he only joined the YMCA in 2023 as a field coordinator, Eddy already holds a symbolic place. “Here, people see me a bit like the dad of the Youth Zone,” he tells us with a broad smile.
Entouré de ses joueurs, le coach élancé: Surrounded by his players, the lanky coach says a few words to them before starting practice. “Congratulations for what you did [in the game] last Friday! I'm so proud of you that I'm telling everyone about it,” he says in a calm voice. “Even if there was a loss, what you did last Friday was really impressive!” the coach says.
Des sourires s’affichent sur le visage d: Smiles spread across the players' faces, and they gradually join in Eddy's applause. Then they go take their positions on the court.
Nous nous installons dans une salle anne: We settle into a side room off the gym to hear the coach's story, which tells how a difficult time at school and his passion for basketball led him to commit himself to youth work.
<strong>« C’était soit l’armée, soit le: “It was either the army or Canada”
Sa peau mate, Eddy la doit à ses origine: Eddy owes his olive skin to his Italian roots and the sun of southern France. That's where he grew up until he was 15, before moving to Montréal with his mother in the 1990s.
Adolescent, Eddy ne supporte pas le syst: As a teenager, Eddy couldn't stand the school system. “I didn't give a damn about school! I had no motivation to go,” he says solemnly. That carefree attitude toward studies often cast him as the class clown. “I wasn't into delinquency, but I was into goofing around a lot. And I really liked girls,” he says, tilting his head from one side to the other, as if to emphasize his point.
Lorsque sa mère évoque la possibilité de: When his mother brought up the possibility of leaving for Canada, Eddy saw an opportunity to begin a new chapter, far from the obstacles he was facing in France. “I wasn't good at school at all, so it was either the army or Canada,” he says bluntly. The idea of a fresh start revived a sense of hope in him, especially when he thought about how important basketball is in North America. Since the age of 12, Eddy had indeed nurtured a passion for the sport. A love that comes from his mother, herself a former national-level player in Lyon, France.
« Le basket m’a sauvé », affirme-t-il en: “Basketball saved me,” he says, bringing a hand to his heart. The orange ball not only kept him from dropping out of school, but also from sinking into the pitfalls of the street. “In the Canadian school system, you play for your school. If you don't go to school, you don't play. And that helped me.”
« Ma première année en tant qu’équipier: “My first year as a teammate in Montréal, I didn't get to play a single game. I had to earn my place. Even though some players were less skilled than me, I stayed on the bench,” Eddy recalls, nodding. “But the next year, I made the starting five,” he adds.
Ces leçons, Eddy n’est pas près de les o: Eddy isn't about to forget those lessons. He played until he was 32, then wanted to pass on to young people the values he himself had learned on the court. “You learn perseverance, you learn respect for others, you learn to recognize another person's qualities, you discover your own qualities, and you also learn to keep quiet,” he lists, talking with his hands. For him, basketball is also a way to teach young people to respect authority figures. “On the court, you can compare the referee to the police. You have to respect them,” he points out.
À 24 ans, Eddy se lance dans l’intervent: At 24, Eddy got into youth work without a university degree, but with solid experience as a day camp counsellor. He also draws his strength from his role as big brother and big cousin in his family. “I'm the oldest in my family. I've always been surrounded by my little cousins, my little brothers. And I've always loved the team spirit,” he explains, his eyes laughing.
Eddy se souvient très bien de sa premièr: Eddy remembers his first experience as a youth worker very well. With a small smile, he says: “It was at La Piaule, in the 2000s, a time when the Beaubien–Jean-Talon neighbourhood was heavily plagued by gangs, so I learned fast on the ground,” he shares. “There were a lot of fights, fires, stabbings on the basketball court,” he lists in a steady rhythm.
Cette première année mouvementée ne l’a: Yet that turbulent first year didn't discourage him. On the contrary, it helped him understand youth better. “All of that, those are situations that teach you an enormous amount. Without waiting for the police to step in, we tried to solve the problems.”
Bien que son métier puisse comporter des: Although his job can involve risks, Eddy says he has never been assaulted or threatened by the young people. He attributes this to the relationship of mutual respect he has always cultivated with them.
Pour Eddy, établir une relation de respe: For Eddy, building a relationship of mutual respect between teenagers and adults isn't limited to his work: it's a philosophy of life. But in his view, this approach is far from being shared. “Spending time with young people, I quickly realized that adults don't respect them. People often say you have to get down to the level of toddlers to understand them, and it's just as important with teenagers,” he insists.
Son constat est clair : il y a un malais: His observation is clear: there is an intergenerational unease. “Far too often, adults look down on teenagers,” Eddy laments, puffing out his chest to illustrate his words. He continues: “Teens aren't often listened to. Yet, often, they're much more open than we are. We have to listen to them.”
Pour lui, comprendre le langage des jeun: For him, understanding young people's language in order to act better is just as important. “I try to teach my youth workers that just because they insult each other, or one of them slaps another on the head, it doesn't mean you need to get worked up. It's not the fight of the year, no!” he exclaims.
Lorsqu’on demande à Eddy de quoi il tire: When Eddy is asked what he takes pride in at work, the youth worker speaks with admiration about the paths some young people have taken. “I'm proud of a lot of [them]. Some are immigrants, they arrive here, their parents don't speak French, but they manage to seize the opportunities that come their way.”
Parmi les jeunes qu’Eddy a côtoyés, un e: Among the young people Eddy has spent time with, one in particular left a mark. “One year, I worked at Lucien-Pagé school. I was in the middle of the school. I had an office and I took the students who were about to drop out,” he says. There he met a teenager who came to his office every lunchtime to write and talk with him.
Il écrivait avec passion, raconte Eddy :: He wrote with passion, Eddy says: about religion, globalization, how he perceived his own identity as a Moroccan immigrant. “But he was a kid who was in trouble. He stole iPhones. I often heard his name, the police came for him,” Eddy remembers, his eyes narrowed.
Quatre ans plus tard, Eddy recroise son: Four years later, Eddy ran into his former student on the streets of Montréal. What he learned on that occasion touched him deeply. During our conversation, he relives the scene: “He told me he could never thank me enough for what I had done for him. And I was thinking, OK, but why? When he showed me his videos, I saw he had over 300,000 views on YouTube! Wow!” he says, his eyes still narrowed, his hand under his chin.
Celui qui avait autrefois lutté pour tro: The young man who had once struggled to find his place in society had become the rapper MB, of the group 514.
Eddy poursuit : « Et ma plus grosse fier: Eddy continues: “And my greatest pride is going to Damso's concert and seeing him on stage doing the opening act. When he saw me, he came down off the stage and gave me a hug,” he shares, the hair standing up on his arms. He thinks for a few seconds, then adds: “I'm proud because that kid wasn't made for the school system. He understood that very quickly, and despite his run-ins with the police, he never gave up and he became a rapper.”
« J’ai dû rencontrer dans ma vie peut-êt: “In my life I must have met maybe 3,000 young people. I'm not going to help everyone. I'm here to give them keys. But sometimes, they won't open the door,” he explains figuratively.
L’intervenant jeunesse souhaite passer u: The youth worker wants to get an important message across: “In high school, nobody's asking you to give 150%. Just do the minimum to get through school, try to see it through to the end. School gives you a diploma, which is already an achievement in itself,” he says, his gaze steady.
« Mais si tu restes allongé dans ton lit: “But if you stay lying in your bed, someone else will take your place. There are more than eight billion people in the world. As soon as I started moving, my life started moving too. The young people I saw move a little succeeded. So my best advice is to get moving,” he drops.
« Si tu ne fais rien, alors tu n’auras r: “If you do nothing, then you'll get nothing. If you don't take your shot with three seconds left in the game, you can be sure you won't win your game,” he finishes passionately.
